title: T-2 toxin-induced neurotoxicity in juvenile rats involves hippocampal oxidative stress-ER stress-mediated neuronal apoptosis and potential gut-brain axis involvement.
authors: Zhou Junfeng; Ma Jiayi; Wang Hongyu; Meng Fanshuang; Li Qingwen et al.
abstract: T-2 toxin, a common Fusarium-derived mycotoxin, poses severe threats to livestock production and public health and exhibits potent neurotoxicity by disrupting blood-brain barrier integrity and neuronal function. However, the detailed mechanisms responsible for its developmental neurotoxicity remain poorly elucidated. This study investigated cognitive impairment and associated central and peripheral alterations in juvenile rats following subchronic T-2 toxin exposure. Juvenile male Wistar rats were orally exposed to T-2 toxin for 28 days. Behavioral, histopathological, microbiome, biochemical, and molecular analyses were performed to evaluate cognitive function, hippocampal injury, intestinal barrier integrity, and gut microbial alterations. T-2 toxin exposure significantly impaired learning, memory, recognition ability, and exploratory behavior. Hippocampal neuronal loss, Nissl body reduction, and endoplasmic reticulum dilation were observed following exposure. T-2 toxin disrupted hippocampal redox homeostasis, as evidenced by increased ROS and MDA levels and decreased SOD activity and GSH content. These changes were accompanied by activation of the PERK-eIF2α-ATF4-CHOP signaling pathway and enhanced neuronal apoptosis. In parallel, T-2 toxin altered gut microbial composition, induced colonic injury, reduced ZO-1 and Occludin expression, and triggered systemic inflammatory imbalance. Collectively, these findings indicate that T-2 toxin-induced cognitive impairment in juvenile rats is associated with oxidative stress-triggered ER stress and neuronal apoptosis in the hippocampus. Concurrent gut microbiota dysbiosis, intestinal barrier dysfunction, and inflammatory alterations suggest a potential contribution of gut-brain interactions to developmental T-2 toxin neurotoxicity. These findings expand current understanding of developmental T-2 toxin neurotoxicity by integrating hippocampal oxidative stress-ER stress signaling with gut microbial and intestinal alterations.

title: Immunological Mechanisms Underlying Cutaneous Immune-Related Adverse Events of Immune Checkpoint Inhibitors: From Shared Antitumor Immunity to Mechanistic Endotypes and Biomarker Discovery.
authors: Pu Tianshu; Teng Yaru; Zhang Yuezhu; Da Meihong; Wang Fei
abstract: Cutaneous immune-related adverse events (cirAEs) are among the most frequent toxicities of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy and often provide an early, clinically visible indication of immune activation. Their occurrence has been associated with favorable antitumor outcomes, particularly for vitiligo-like depigmentation, raising the possibility that skin toxicity and therapeutic efficacy share biological determinants. However, cirAEs comprise a heterogeneous spectrum, and the mechanisms linking checkpoint blockade to distinct cutaneous phenotypes remain incompletely defined. Here, we propose a framework in which ICI therapy alters immune regulation and promotes immune activation through partially overlapping pathways, while antigen specificity, effector-cell polarization, tissue-resident immunity, and host factors shape the resulting cutaneous phenotype. We review evidence for tumor-skin antigen cross-reactivity and T-cell clonality, humoral autoimmunity, phenotype-specific cytokine programs, regulatory T-cell dysfunction, tissue-resident memory T cells, and microbial, genetic, and sex-related modifiers. We then distinguish mechanisms shared with antitumor immunity from those that are more specific to tissue injury, and discuss their implications for biomarkers and mechanism-informed treatment. This framework emphasizes that cirAE occurrence may reflect productive immune engagement, whereas phenotype and severity are shaped by additional tissue- and host-specific mechanisms. Better longitudinal and paired tumor-skin studies are needed to translate these observations into predictive biomarkers and antitumor-immunity-sparing interventions.

title: Preoperative anastomotic response microbial subtypes (ARMS) are associated with anastomotic leakage after colorectal cancer surgery
authors: Zafeiropoulou K; Zafeiropoulos H; Liu K; Zwezerijnen-Jiwa FH; Petersen AE et al.
abstract: Anastomotic leakage (AL) is a severe complication following colorectal cancer (CRC) surgery, associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Identifying predictive factors for AL may improve risk stratification and facilitate early diagnosis. In this post hoc exploratory analysis of 421 CRC patients undergoing elective resection with primary anastomosis across two international, multicentre clinical studies, we profiled their preoperative fecal microbiota using 16S rRNA gene sequencing and shotgun metagenomic sequencing. AL occurred in 28 patients (6.7%). Fecal profiling revealed a bimodal distribution of Segatella copri, which served as the foundation for our two-step stratification pipeline. In Step 1, high relative abundance of S. copri was associated with successful anastomotic healing, defining candidate anastomotic response microbial subtype 1 (ARMS-1, low risk). In Step 2, among patients with low S. copri abundance, analysis of microbial metabolic potential identified 165 KEGG orthology (KO) terms enriched in AL patients. Machine learning models trained on these KOs predicted AL with high accuracy, significantly outperforming an externally validated anastomotic leak risk calculator, and differentiating candidate ARMS-2 (medium risk) from ARMS-3 (high risk). In mice, colonization with Palleniella intestinalis, the murine homolog of S. copri, enhanced the expression of transcripts key to barrier integrity, while reducing postoperative circulating markers associated with AL in our human cohort. Overall, this study demonstrates that preoperative fecal microbiome profiling enables accurate AL risk stratification through a functional two-step pipeline and offers mechanistically plausible insights into microbial contributions to anastomotic healing.

title: A draft mouse pangenome graph reference
authors: Macias-Velasco JF; Garza JE; Zhang W; Wu W; Xu Z et al.
abstract: The mouse is a foundational model organism, yet most genomic analyses rely on linear references that fail to capture laboratory-strain genetic diversity. We present three base-level mouse pangenome graphs on the C57BL/6J telomere-to-telomere (mT2T) backbone: a 19-strain draft mouse pangenome; the founder pangenome (FP) of the 8 Collaborative Cross (CC) founders that constitute the CC's enumerable haplotype space; and the CC pangenome, the FP augmented with personalized diploid haplotypes from 40 CC recombinant inbred lines. This personalization recovers per-animal diploid genomes from short-read whole-genome sequencing at 99.2% mean concordance with expected mosaics, with substantial reproducibility in Diversity Outbred animals at very low coverage, providing a cost-effective alternative to per-sample assembly. Alignment to the FP improves both quality and accuracy of read placement compared to GRCm38 or mT2T, reducing reference-allele bias and increasing variant-calling sensitivity. The graphs support haplotype-specific analysis of methylation and allele-specific analysis of expression and chromatin accessibility.
summary_zh: 构建基于mT2T骨架的三种小鼠泛基因组图，整合19品系、8个CC创始者及40个CC重组近交系单倍型，提升比对与变异检测并支持单倍型分析。

title: To sort or to hash? Revisiting k-mer counting
authors: Levallois; V.; Patro; R.; Peterlongo; P.; Pibiri; G. E.
abstract: Motivation: Counting k-mers in large genomic datasets is a foundational primitive in bioinformatics, supporting applications such as genome assembly, variant discovery, metagenomic profiling, and sequence database indexing. As sequencing throughput grows, k-mer counting is routinely applied to collections of hundreds to thousands of files. Even a modest per-file speedup compounds into hours of saved computation across such collections. Methods: Sorting and hashing are the two main ways of counting k-mers, and practice has largely settled on the former, of which KMC3 (Kokot et al., 2017) is the most refined expression. We reconsider this choice and analyze both approaches using a cost model that charges computation and memory transfers together. We show that the outcome of the comparison rests on two matters: how abundant the k-mers are, and whether the hash tables fit in cache. Sorting is faster only when data is mostly unique and the hash tables do not fit in cache. We then design a k-mer counting algorithm in the light of this analysis. We adopt the consolidated paradigm based on first partitioning the k-mers by their minimizer, thus obtaining partitions of super-k-mers, and then counting each partition independently in parallel. In particular, super-k-mers are deduplicated before counting, and the number of partitions is chosen so that the hash tables fit in cache whenever possible. The algorithm avoids writing temporary data to disk if enough internal memory is available. Results: We implemented this strategy in a tool named Tuna and show that it is faster than KMC3 on all but one of our inputs, spanning bacterial and human assemblies, metagenomes and read sets, by up to 4.3x. The advantage of Tuna compared to KMC3 in the counting step alone widens to 6.8x as k-mer abundance grows, as the analysis predicts. On the largest input tested, 614 GB of human sequencing reads, Tuna counts within 4 GB of memory and 0.7 TB of temporary disk. On that input the two tools finish within 1.1x of each other under the full 256 GB budget, and restricting every tool to the same 8 GB budget widens the advantage of Tuna over KMC3 to 1.8x. Software: The software is freely available at github.com/vicLeva/tuna under the MIT license.
summary_zh: 通过成本模型比较排序与哈希，设计minimizer分区和super-k-mer去重的Tuna算法，验证其多数数据上快于KMC3。

title: Deciphering Molecular Language for Spectral Interpretation with a Foundation Model Pretrained on Repository-Wide Metabolomics Data
authors: Li; Y.; Zhong; Y.; Liu; P.; Wang; Z.; Xie et al.
abstract: In-depth, scalable structural interpretation of tandem mass spectra from diverse biological tissues and environmental samples is essential for understanding the molecular diversity of cellular environments and the metabolic architecture of living systems. Although community-driven resources such as GNPS and MassIVE have aggregated massive volumes of tandem mass spectra spanning a wide range of organisms, clinical cohorts and environmental surveys, modeling and interpreting this exponentially expanding spectral corpus to distill molecular information and derive meaningful biological insights poses a fundamental challenge for established computational methods. Here we present UltraMS, a dual-polarity foundation model tailored to decipher the molecular language latent in tandem mass spectra through large-scale pretraining on more than 160 million spectra encompassing both positive and negative ion modes. Our findings illustrate that UltraMS is capable of effectively decoding the chemical semantics of molecules underlying mass spectra via self-supervised learning, achieving superior performance across a variety of downstream tasks, including elemental detection, molecular identification, molecular property profiling, and metabolic landscape characterization. Remarkably, UltraMS enables conducting molecular identification with fine-grained spectral interpretability, simultaneously elucidating molecular structures from untargeted MS/MS spectra and providing peak-by-peak substructural attributions via annotation transfer. Deployed on a clinical cohort of human plaque samples, UltraMS demonstrates significant potential in discovering previously unrecognized phenotype-linked metabolites supported by structurally grounded fragment-ion formation pathways, while effectively correcting likely misannotated clinical markers. Furthermore, building on the structure-aware spectral representations learned by UltraMS, we construct UltraAtlas, a chemical-property-resolved map that organizes millions of experimental spectra into a unified coordinate system, enabling millisecond-scale molecular profiling and offering practical guidance for exploratory navigation across vast chemical space. Applied to human scalp metabolomics, UltraAtlas effectively captures distinct metabolic variations across individuals, highlighting phenotype-specific chemical signatures while shedding light on the chemical niches of the resident microbiome. Together, UltraMS and UltraAtlas constitute a generalizable framework for structural elucidation and biological discovery from tandem mass spectra, empowering the comprehensive exploration of the largely undeciphered metabolomes across different domains of life.

title: Measuring Cell Type Resolved Aging Through Long-Read Sequencing
authors: Wu; Y.; Stevens; H.; Eames; A.; Moqri; M.; Gladyshev et al.
abstract: Epigenetic clocks based on bulk blood DNA methylation are powerful tools for quantifying biological aging, but bulk measurements conflate cell-autonomous epigenetic changes with age-related shifts in blood cell composition. Here, we develop LongReadClock, a set of cell-type-resolved epigenetic aging clocks constructed from cohort-scale long-read whole-genome sequencing of bulk blood without physical cell sorting. Individual sequencing reads were classified using seven target-specific blood-cell models using methylation-based log-likelihood-ratio scoring against a purified-cell atlas. LongReadClock achieved mean absolute errors of 2.8-5.7 years on held-out samples across bulk blood and digitally resolved cell types. Covariate-adjusted analyses identified associations that differed across cell types, including lower mean epigenetic age deviation (EAD) in males in B-cell and NK-cells, associations of systolic blood pressure and resting heart rate with myeloid EAD, and higher NK-cell EAD in participants with asthma. A Fisher-information screen was used to prioritize age-informative genomic windows and to explore read-level methylation patterns at the ELOVL2 locus. These results support cell-type-resolved epigenetic age inference from cohort-scale long-read methylation data from standard bulk blood samples.

title: A 6-week all-liquid caloric restriction diet reduced abundance of some butyrate-producing bacteria while increasing abundance of mucin-degrading bacteria
authors: Dirks; B.; Nirmalkar; K.; Votruba; S.; Hollstein; T.; Krakoff et al.
abstract: Caloric restriction diets are a common diet strategy to reduce excess weight and obesity. The diets work by lowering the number of calories or energy input below a human's normal energy expenditure creating an energy deficit. Caloric restriction diet meals can be composed of whole foods, meal replacement shakes, or a combination of the two. While the effects of these diets on human metabolism are well-known, the effects of these diets and the durability of these effects on the human gut microbiome are less well-known. The objective of this work was to investigate the effects of a 6-week all-liquid caloric restriction diet on the human gut microbiota using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing to assess changes in diversity, community composition, and predicted function. We found that during the diet period beta-diversity shifts significantly away from what it was before the intervention (baseline), and returns to baseline a week after the diet. During the diet period we also observed a decrease in abundance of fiber-degrading and butyrate-producing bacteria with a simultaneous increase in abundance of mucin-degrading bacteria with a return to baseline level abundances in the post-diet period. Despite a liquid diet relatively high in carbohydrate (59% carbohydrate, 25% fat, 16% protein), predicted function analysis showed a shift in substrate preference away from dietary carbohydrates towards protein and host-glycans during the diet period. These findings suggest that despite the overall high carbohydrate content all-liquid caloric restriction diets deprive the gut microbiota of their preferred nutrient source due to the overall decline in calorie delivery which forces them to consume alternative nutrient sources like protein and host-glycans.

title: A refined InDel taxonomy broadens the repertoire of mutational processes shaping multiple myeloma
authors: Papadimitriou; M.; Pandey; A.; Poos; A.; Becker; N.; Alaoui et al.
abstract: Somatic aberrations have been extensively characterized in multiple myeloma (MM). However, the mutational processes underlying small insertions and deletions (InDels) remain poorly understood. Here, we used a recently developed 89-channel InDel classification schema which allows differentiating mutational processes. We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from 887 MM samples, spanning both newly diagnosed (NDMM) and relapsed/refractory disease (RRMM). We identified InDel signatures associated with replication slippage, APOBEC mutagenesis, topoisomerase 1 (TOP1)-mediated mutagenesis, non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), and two rare DNA damage repair-deficiency signatures. In two randomized clinical trials, incorporation of the APOBEC InDel signature InD9a improved treatment outcome prediction as pertaining to progression-free survival (PFS) and achievement of minimal residual disease (MRD) negativity. InD29, a signature linked to NHEJ-mediated errors, was detected in both NDMM and RRMM, and was enriched in samples exhibiting melphalan-associated mutagenesis and high SV burden. Genome-wide analysis identified a recurrent InDel hotspot at TXNDC5, a highly expressed gene in MM located within a region implicated in complex genomic rearrangements, with predominantly noncoding alterations suggesting potential regulatory consequences. Finally, InDel signatures revealed the presence of mismatch-repair deficiency (MMRd) and homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) phenotypes, even in cases without germline predisposition. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive characterization of InDel mutagenesis in MM, revealing previously underexplored relationships and demonstrating potential to refine comprehensive genomic classifications of MM.

title: Fast draft assemblies using locally consistent parsing
authors: Karaoglanoglu; F.; Zambaku; K.; Ashyralyyev; A.; Ebren; E.; Nappi et al.
abstract: Recent improvements in long-read sequencing accuracy, particularly the introduction of PacBio HiFi reads, have created new opportunities for more efficient sequence representations in genome assembly. In particular, variations of de Bruijn graphs (dBG), such as sparse dBG and minimizer-space dBG, provide efficient representations of sequences and have enabled genome assemblers to leverage the high accuracy of long-read data while maintaining low memory usage and fast analysis times. Locally consistent parsing (LCP) is another technique for compact sequence representation that partitions a string into nearly uniform, highly distinctive substrings in a consistent manner. In this work, we combine ideas from minimizer-space assembly and LCP to achieve a significant speedup in HiFi long-read assembly. Specifically, we define a locally consistent de Bruijn Graph (lcDBG), in which string partitions serve as the graph's building blocks. We introduce Gallifrey, a rapid PacBio HiFi assembler that outperforms the fastest existing tool, rust-mdbg, by >6x in runtime while requiring 2x less memory, assembling a human genome in under one minute on a standard laptop, while generating assemblies with comparable contiguity. Code for Gallifrey is freely available at https://github.com/BilkentCompGen/gallifrey.
summary_zh: 提出基于局部一致解析的Gallifrey组装器，实现HiFi长读长快速低内存的人类基因组草图组装。

title: Unipept in 2026: A Unified Web Platform for Comparative Metaproteomics Analysis
authors: Vande Moortele; T.; Van de Vyver; S.; Binke; B.-B.; Van Den Bossche; T.; Martens et al.
abstract: Metaproteomics studies the collective proteome of microbial communities to characterize their taxonomic composition and functional activity. Unipept has long supported such analyses, but organizing samples into projects, building targeted reference databases, and comparing samples across a study were only possible in a standalone desktop application. Here we present a major update that moves these workflows into the web application, so a complete multi-sample study can be assembled, analyzed, and shared without local installation. Samples can be compared both taxonomically and functionally, the latter by mapping enzymes onto metabolic pathways with the integrated PathwayPilot. The analyses also became more informative. The Peptonizer2000, now accelerated by the new NORI inference engine, adds confidence scores to taxonomic and functional results, and an optional filter removes common contaminants before analysis. The Unipept API itself was also reworked, with an optimized index and flexible memory loading that roughly doubled query throughput and lowered the memory needed for deployment. We demonstrate these capabilities on six datasets of a defined microbial community.

title: Evaluating WGS-based methods as an in silico replacement of phage typing for historical continuity and host association in  Salmonella Typhimurium
authors: Kolodziejczyk; G. M.; Guzinski; J.; Wanelik; K. M.; Arnold; M.; Couto Alves et al.
abstract: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) poses a significant burden on public health worldwide. The Anderson phage typing scheme has historically supported surveillance, outbreak investigations and source attribution through associations between phage types and animal hosts. However, limitations inherent to the scheme have led to the gradual replacement of phage typing by whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based methods. In this study, we applied statistical and machine learning approaches to 1,329 high-quality STm whole-genome sequences to compare phage typing with hierarchical clustering of core-genome multilocus sequence typing (HierCC) and the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) address. We observed low congruence (< 0.60) between phage typing and WGS-based approaches. Nevertheless, a random forest model using WGS-based subtypes as features was able to predict all phage types with high specificity ([≥] 0.94) and at least 80% recall for 10 of the 24 analysed phage types. These included phage types of human and veterinary epidemiological importance, including DT193, DT104, DT2, DT40, DT56, DT9, and DT99. We then assessed whether WGS-based subtyping methods could replace the host-association feature of phage typing. At higher distance thresholds ([≥] 100) WGS-based subtyping methods were more informative of animal host species and displayed stronger host-associations than phage types for 11 of the 12 animal hosts, with significantly stronger associations for ducks, finches, and pigs (all p < 0.05). Thus, despite low congruence between phage types and WGS-based subtypes, our random forest model accurately predicted several epidemiologically important phage types, including those important to public health and veterinary surveillance, supporting its potential as an in silico alternative for those phage types. Finally, our findings suggest HierCC and SNP address methods can capture the host-association information historically derived from phage typing.

title: An Exponential Scale Mixture Model for Metatranscriptomics Data with Application to Inflammatory Bowel Disease
abstract: Metatranscriptomic (MTX) sequencing profiles gene expression across microbial communities, but differential expression analysis is challenging because the abundances are non-negative, extremely sparse, and right-skewed. Standard MTX pipelines output normalized abundances rather than raw counts, limiting the direct use of RNA-seq count-based methods. Gaussian methods require data transformation with pseudocounts, which can lead to distributional misspecification and pseudocount sensitivity. We develop an exponential scale mixture (ESM) framework that directly models MTX abundances with an interpretable mean regression structure while accommodating near-zero concentration and heavy right tails. The complete ESM model, incorporating a two-component mixture and a left-censoring mechanism, can account for extreme sparsity and assign positive probability to observed zeros. In simulation studies, the ESM achieved greater power at comparable empirical false discovery rates (FDRs), more accurate signal strength estimation, better distributional fit, and better FDR calibration than a representative Gaussian alternative. In a case study using inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) multi-omics data, the ESM and the Gaussian model identified markedly different sets of genes (230 vs. 927), while distributional diagnostics strongly favored the ESM. The greater FDR inflation of the Gaussian model in simulations warrants caution in interpreting its larger discovery set. Functional annotation mapped several ESM-exclusive discoveries to gene families associated with IBD-related functions, while Pfam enrichment identified a significant functional signature involving phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP)-utilizing enzymes.

title: An intragastric murine model that recapitulates natural infection with invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella for preclinical evaluation of vaccine immunogenicity and protection
authors: Mocci; V.; Fiorino; F.; Tambassi; M.; D'annunzio; G.; Mazzera et al.
abstract: Invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease is a major global health concern, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where young children and immunocompromised individuals are particularly vulnerable. Preclinical models that reproduce the natural course of invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella infection without antibiotic-mediated disruption of the intestinal microbiota are essential for vaccine development. Here, an antibiotic-free murine model is described based on intragastric infection of susceptible C57BL/6 mice with the ST313 clinical isolate Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium D23580. Over seven days, infection progressed from intestinal colonization to extraintestinal dissemination, accompanied by increasing histopathological damage and activation of local and systemic inflammatory responses. The ability of the infection model to evaluate vaccine-induced immunity and protection was assessed by immunizing mice with a formalin-inactivated D23580 strain. Vaccination elicited Salmonella-specific serum IgG and reduced clinical severity, with vaccinated mice showing significantly lower bacterial loads in blood, liver and colon compared with control mice after intragastric challenge. By combining the enteric route, which mimics the natural route of human infection, with an intact intestinal microbiota, this model reproduces key features of progressive invasive non-typhoidal Salmonella disease and provides a tool for investigating host-pathogen interactions and evaluating vaccine-induced immunity and protection.

title: A configuration-resolved benchmark of differential abundance analysis methods for human gut 16S rRNA microbiome data
authors: Abdelmalek; N.; Di Meo; C.; Fiorito; G.; Uzzau; S.; Tanca et al.
abstract: Differential abundance (DA) analysis decides which taxa a 16S rRNA study reports. Each DA tool runs under choices of normalisation, transformation, zero handling and reference, yet benchmarks usually compare tools at their defaults. We benchmarked 11 tools in 43 configurations on 1,064 datasets, with signals implanted into healthy stool and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) mucosal profiles or data simulated from the stool profiles, and in two real cohorts with permuted labels. Designs varied sample size, effect size, signal structure, confounding and read depth. The study design explained most of the variation in the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), followed by the tool and, much less, by its configuration. A few settings changed error control as much as the choice of tool, including the sensitivity analysis of ANCOM-BC2, median comparison in MaAsLin 3 and zero handling in LinDA. Linear models, mostly on log scales with a small pseudo-count, gave the highest MCC at an empirical false discovery rate (FDR) near the nominal level. Empirical FDR exceeded the nominal level for negative binomial count models, and for methods testing proportions in larger studies and under shifts in one direction. Fixed pseudo-counts on log-ratio scales failed when read depth differed about 1.35-fold between groups, and references assuming most taxa unchanged failed when most taxa shifted. The ranking held across taxonomic levels, communities and simulations, and agreed with how liberal each configuration was on permuted sex and IBD labels. We derive recommendations for gut 16S studies and a permutation check applicable to any dataset.

title: OTU Taxa: a taxonomy aware pretrained model for 16S microbiome profiles
authors: Henao; R.; Hoehndorf; R.; Perez Nastar; H. D.
abstract: Background: Microbiome profiles combine sequence-derived units with taxonomy. Pretrained models use different community vocabularies and are often evaluated on few labels, leaving their value under broad competitive evaluation unclear. We introduce OTU-Taxa, which pairs operational taxonomic unit (OTU) identity with hierarchical taxonomy during autoregressive pretraining on unlabeled profiles. Results: In an in-domain evaluation across 250 Microbe Atlas Project (MAP)-derived classification tasks with disjoint folds, mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.744 for OTU-Taxa and 0.749 for Random Forest. OTU-Taxa was the highest-ranked pretrained method; Nemenyi comparisons did not detect rank differences from Random Forest across the three metrics. The model also generated largely non-copied profiles and recovered more withheld community members at larger cutoffs, while retrieval gave stronger empirical fidelity and early ranking. It also supported abundance-rank readouts and recovered higher-rank classifier assignments from sample context for known-vocabulary OTUs under controlled sequence degradation, although agreement was limited at genus and species ranks. Conclusions: Within the MAP 97% closed-reference 16S vocabulary, the pretrained representation supports in-domain prediction of metadata labels alongside generative and taxonomic readouts. Supervised abundance models, empirical retrieval, and intact-sequence classifiers remain stronger choices for several corresponding endpoints, while OTU-Taxa provides one shared contextual representation across all four analyses.

title: A distributed, privacy-preserving platform for linkage of epidemiological data with pathogen genome sequences
authors: Langevin; J.; Featherstone; L.; Di Giallonardo; F.; Horsburgh; B. A.; Lloyd et al.
abstract: Efficient and secure integration of epidemiological data with pathogen genome sequence data is essential for identifying genetic clusters, monitoring emerging mutations and targeting public health responses. However, this information is often collected across different organisations: epidemiological data is collected by public health units while genome sequence data is collected by diagnostic laboratories. Linking these sources often requires manual or semi-manual approaches, leading to unnecessary delays in identifying emerging outbreaks. To address this, we developed a proof-of-concept privacy-preserving distributed platform, SecureEpiLink, for automatic linkage of pathogen genome sequences and notification data across public health and diagnostic laboratories. SecureEpiLink uses cryptographic hashing to establish linkage, without exposing personal identifying information. This ensures that the resulting linked data can be used to identify the emergence of genetic clusters without identification of individuals comprising each cluster, with the original identifiable data remaining stored at source units. We benchmarked SecureEpiLink against manual linkage and another linkage service using HIV and HCV datasets from New South Wales, Australia. SecureEpiLink performed similarly to manual linkage and outperformed previously used linkage algorithms, with all errors attributable to data entry errors in the underlying dataset. Lastly, we demonstrate how SecureEpiLink can be integrated with automated genomic epidemiology pipelines. SecureEpiLink is available from https://github.com/jolenefarrell/SecureEpiLink.
